title: How Senior Leaders Can Lead Learning in Schools
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes sets out a model for instructional leadership built around five aligned elements - vision, curriculum, teaching, assessment and development - arguing leaders should ask where the system is least aligned rather than simply what they observed in a lesson. She distinguishes a compliance culture, which checks whether learning walks and data drops happened, from an improvement culture, which asks what those activities actually changed. She warns that shared frameworks for classroom quality (such as her own All Saints MAT pillars) become dangerous when reduced to 'spot the technique' games rather than tools for diagnosing learning problems. The piece reframes quality assurance as a hypothesis-testing cycle - diagnose, gather evidence, develop, implement, review - that is only complete when teaching changes and pupils learn more, not merely when evidence has been collected.
points: Hughes's alignment model (vision, curriculum, teaching, assessment, development) reframes the leader's core question from 'what did I see?' to 'where is the system least aligned?'

She distinguishes compliance culture (did the activity happen?) from improvement culture (did the activity change adult action and pupil learning?), a sharp diagnostic for auditing leadership practice.
Her warning that technique-frameworks can become a 'game of spot the technique' cautions leaders against mistaking visible strategy use for genuine instructional quality.
She reframes QA as hypothesis-testing: evidence should be chosen specifically to test a diagnosis, and the loop is complete only when pupil learning improves, not when evidence is collected.
quotes: The most important question for a senior leader is not, 'What did I see?' but, 'Where is the system least aligned?'
A compliance culture asks whether learning walks have happened, whether data has been entered and whether meetings have taken place. An improvement culture asks what those activities changed.

Cold calling is not effective because it is visible during an observation. It is effective when it increases thinking, makes participation more equitable and helps the teacher gather information about understanding.

If Year 10 outcomes in a subject are weaker than expected, leaders should resist jumping straight to more monitoring or more intervention. They might instead ask whether pupils are failing to remember core knowledge.
The loop is not complete when evidence has been collected. It is complete when teaching changes and pupils know, remember or can do more.
